Thangka. Hanging - Lamaist hanging or ' tanka' . " This is a printed ' tanka' (Tibetan ' thang- ka'), usually kept in a temple. The general style of the ' tanka' is in the Tibetan tradition, but there are several aspects which are characteristically Mongolian, particularly the prayers in Mongol script down the sides and bottom, and the representation of a Mongol felt tent ('ger') centre left. The ' tanka' represents the Green Tara (centre), seated on a lotus and holding in her left hand a long- stemmed lotus flower. She is the consort of Avalokita, now thought to be incarnate in the Dalai Lamas, and she is one of the most popular deities in Tibet and Mongolia, both with Lamas and laity. The green version of Tara is more common than the white version, which according to Waddell, is believed by the Mongols to be incarnate in the White Tsar. This ' tanka' has nine Taras (a much more common number is twenty-one, each of which has a particular quality for helping people. The ' tanka' represent,apart from the Taras: the sun (right) and the moon (left), temples, snakes, camels and riders, etc. Centre top is (probably) the demon Damdin, defender of the faith, or Lha- mo, a demoness defender of the faith. The deity is surrounded by flames, indicating that it is one of the fierce deities, riding a horse, and slaying a ?dragon. Centre bottom is (probably) the female deity Narici, meaning ' the resplendent', a goddess of the dawn. She is linked with the pig, and here she is seated in a chariot drawn by pigs. In her usual form she has three faces and eight hands, but here she seems to have only one face and two hands. She holds various weapons in her hands; in her fiercer forms she is the companion of the warrior-Damdin. Sometimes she is called ' the diamond sow' . Many scenes in this ' tanka' remain unexplained, such as the two figures left bottom kneeling beside one another, or the strangely medieval boats on a lake right centre-bottom. The ' tanka' was obtained from Buryat ASSR, in 1972, but it is not known if it was manufactured there or in Mongolia."
